The Fastrac turbine is required to produce 895 kW of power and spins at 20,000 RPM.
The turbine has 24 converging-diverging nozzles, 147 impulse-type shrouded blades, and 67 exit guide vanes (EGVs).
The nozzle exit Mach number is predicted to be 2.11, with a total-to-static pressure ratio of 11.2 across the nozzle.
The small nozzle-to-blade gap case (0.102 cm) predicted a work output of 276.3 kJ/kg and a power output of 890 kW.
The large nozzle-to-blade gap case (0.838 cm) predicted a work output of 269.1 kJ/kg and a power output of 867 kW.
The uncoupled nozzle and blade/EGV simulation under-predicted the losses and did not accurately capture the mixing and unsteadiness in the axial gap region.
The modal analysis of the turbine blades indicated possible resonance near the nominal design speed due to excitations from the nozzle count and the EGVs.
The unsteady CFD analysis showed high levels of unsteadiness at the blade leading edge, particularly at the nozzle passing frequency and its second harmonic.
Increasing the nozzle-to-blade gap reduced the unsteadiness at the nozzle passing frequency but increased unsteadiness at the second harmonic.
The CFD grid had a total of 1,545,987 grid points, with 41 radial planes, chosen based on a compromise between accuracy and computational time.
The numerical algorithm used was third-order spatially accurate and second-order temporally accurate, with two Newton sub-iterations per time step.
The turbulent viscosity was calculated using the two-layer Baldwin-Lomax algebraic turbulence model.
Message Passing Interface (MPI) software was implemented to enable parallel processing and reduce computational run times.
The unsteady CFD analysis provided data to support the aerodynamic and structural dynamic assessments of the turbine design.
The authors plan to perform further studies on the effects of different nozzle-to-blade axial spacings and the detailed flow physics in the axial gap region.
